tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'19 paper (PDF linked from the benchmark_url page) reports numeric wins against Linux and ZygOS on stated hardware (Xeon E5-2650v4, Intel 82599ES). The repo has benchmark code (apps/synthetic with linux-server/linux-client modes, apps/bench with gcc/g++ -O3 Makefiles), but the paper states no compiler versions or flags, and none for the baseline builds (memcached 1.5.6, gdnsd 2.4.0, ZygOS/Linux spin-servers from the ZygOS repo), so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: memcached (USR workload): Shenango handles over 5 million requests/s with 37 us median and 93 us 99.9th-percentile latency, keeping 99.9th-percentile latency below 100 us at 'one million more than ZygOS' (ZygOS keeps similar response times only up to ~4 million requests/s). Linux memcached reaches about 800,000 requests/s before 99th-percentile latency spikes (no batch work). With batch work, Linux's 99.9th-percentile latency at 0.4M requests/s goes from 83 us to over 2 ms. gdnsd DNS over UDP: Linux up to 900,000 requests/s (41 us median) vs Shenango 5.7 million requests/s, 'a 6.33x improvement' (36 us median, 73 us 99.9th percentile). Thread microbenchmarks (Table 2): spawn-join 148 ns vs 12,996 ns with Linux pthreads; condvar ping-pong 100 ns vs 1,900 ns. Per the abstract, unlike ZygOS, Shenango can linearly trade latency-sensitive throughput for batch-processing throughput.
corrections.workload: memcached 1.5.6 USR workload (99.8% GET / 0.2% SET) over TCP; Rust spin-server with constant/exponential/bimodal service times (10 us mean); gdnsd 2.4.0 DNS over UDP. Each runs alongside PARSEC swaptions batch work, with 1,200 persistent connections from 6 client machines and all systems limited to 16 hyperthreads. Also load-burst tests (100k to 5M requests/s) and thread-operation microbenchmarks vs pthreads, Go and Arachne. Core reallocation every 5 us.
corrections.hardware: Dual-socket server with 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2650v4 @ 2.20 GHz (first socket only, hyper-threads on, TurboBoost, C-states and frequency scaling disabled), 64 GB RAM, 10 Gb/s Intel 82599ES NIC; Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.15.0 (ZygOS on Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.11.0); load from six quad-core machines through a Mellanox SX1024 switch with ConnectX-3 Pro NICs
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. Repo Makefiles: gcc (runtime/IOKernel) and g++ (apps/bench) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -mssse3 (non-DEBUG build); Rust apps built with cargo --release on nightly. No compiler versions given.
corrections.caveats: The README says 'This repository is no longer maintained' and points to the successor shenango/caladan. The last commit (2024-11-05) only adds that README notice, so the entry stays marked abandoned. By commit age alone (about 23 months) the rule would give 'stale'. The benchmark_url abstract page has only the qualitative claim; the numbers are in the paper PDF. ZygOS reaches higher peak memcached throughput than Shenango, but at a high latency cost. At memcached's very short service times (<2 us) the IOKernel becomes the bottleneck. Shenango dedicates a full core (2 hyperthreads) to the IOKernel. The main win is CPU efficiency (batch throughput recovered) at equal tail latency, not raw speed over kernel-bypass stacks. The successor Caladan (shenango/caladan, Apache-2.0, 200 stars, pushed 2026-09-25) was published at OSDI'20, not NSDI'20: https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/fried. Its abstract claims an 11,000x tail-latency reduction vs Parties (580 ms to 52 us).

notes: Tier B confirmed, and numbers are now filled in from the paper PDF. The strongest baseline number is 6.33x DNS throughput vs Linux gdnsd. The abandoned tag is kept because the maintainers' README declares it unmaintained; by the commit-age rule alone it would be 'stale', so the orchestrator may want to decide. Caladan (OSDI'20, with numbers) may deserve its own entry; the searcher's 404 came from using the wrong venue (NSDI'20).

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The peer-reviewed SOSP'21 paper is open access (author-hosted PDF) and reports numeric wins against the Linux kernel sockets/epoll path: echo RTT, UDP relay latency, Redis throughput and an Azure VM run. Hardware is stated (Xeon Silver 4114, Mellanox CX-5) and the code is public on GitHub, but the paper gives no compiler/toolchain version or build flags, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SOSP'21 paper, 64 B echo RTT on Linux hosts (Fig. 5): Linux POSIX 30.4 us vs Catnip (DPDK) UDP 6.0 us + 0.025 us of Demikernel time, Catnip TCP 7.1 + 0.053 us, Catmint (RDMA) 5.3 + 0.949 us. That is about 4.3-5x lower RTT with Catnip (derived from page data). UDP relay server (Fig. 10): average 24.9 us on Linux vs 13.9 us on Catnip, p99 27.6 vs 14.9 us; the paper says 'Catnip reduces the server-side latency per request by 11us on average and 13.7us at the p99' (io_uring: 24.4/25.8 us). Redis in-memory peak throughput vs unmodified Redis on Linux (Fig. 11): 'Catmint gives 2x throughput, and Catnip offers 20% better throughput'. Azure VM: 'Catnip offers a 5x latency improvement over the Linux kernel'. The 2019 first-party blog (CloudLab Redis) says '60% of the latency comes from the OS kernel and its interface' (30% from interface inefficiency, another 30% removed by RDMA/DPDK kernel bypass).
corrections.workload: SOSP'21: 64 B echo server/client (1M echos, 5 runs); UDP relay (TURN) server driven by a Linux traffic generator; Redis via redis-benchmark GET/SET (64 B values, 1M keys, in-memory and with a per-SET fsync append-only log); TxnStore under YCSB-t. Compared against Linux POSIX sockets/epoll, io_uring and kernel-bypass systems (eRPC, Shenango, Caladan, DPDK testpmd, RDMA perftest). The 2019 blog ran the Redis benchmark on CloudLab.
corrections.hardware: SOSP'21 Linux cluster: 5 servers with 20-core dual-socket Intel Xeon Silver 4114 @ 2.2 GHz, Mellanox CX-5 100 Gbps NICs, Arista 7060CX 100 Gbps switch, Intel Optane 800P NVMe. Windows cluster: 14-core dual-socket Xeon 2690 @ 2.6 GHz with Mellanox CX-4 56 Gbps. The 2019 blog used CloudLab with a 25Gb network and Mellanox CX-4 NICs.
corrections.caveats: The SOSP'21 paper is open access at the first author's site; the ACM DL PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, but the paper is not paywalled. The wins are against the Linux kernel sockets/epoll path. Against other kernel-bypass stacks Demikernel is competitive rather than uniformly faster: Catnip echo is 1.7 us slower than Caladan, Catnip (UDP) reaches 70% of Caladan's peak throughput, and Catmint reaches 46% of eRPC's. The Linux-sockets LibOS (Catnap) busy-polls a full core and has lower Redis peak throughput than unmodified Redis. The gains need DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs, and the README calls the project a prototype with no guarantees. The paper states no Rust/compiler version or build flags.

notes: Upgraded C->B through the open-access SOSP'21 paper, which has concrete numbers vs Linux: about 5x echo RTT, 2x Redis throughput with RDMA, and 5x on an Azure VM. The blog's 30%/60% figures are quoted correctly. Metadata checked: MIT, 1,238 stars, last default-branch (dev) commit 2025-11-12, so 'active' holds; the repo pushed_at of 2026-07-23 comes from a non-default branch.
